01

The Python program

My Python program takes two masses and their separation through a Tkinter interface. It calculates their gravitational attraction and updates their velocities and positions over small time steps. Matplotlib draws their trails.

The plot has three axes, but the initial velocities in the supplied program keep the motion in a plane.

A JavaScript adaptation for this website, using velocity-Verlet integration. The downloadable Python program is unchanged and uses a different integration method.

02

How it moves the bodies

The original program calculates force with Newton’s inverse-square law. It updates velocity first, then uses that new velocity to move each body: a semi-implicit Euler step.

force = G * m1 * m2 / distance**2
vel1[i] += force / m1 * d[i] / distance * dt
pos1[i] += vel1[i] * dt

The browser model instead uses velocity-Verlet: update positions with the current acceleration, calculate the new acceleration, then update velocity using their average. The fixed numerical timestep stays the same when you change playback speed.

03

What it doesn't do

These are point masses with exaggerated visual sizes. There are no surface collisions, other planets, or relativistic effects. The energy drift number shows how much error the math is building up.
